profile.title: Infinite Number of Order Parameters for Spin-Glasses
profile.canonical_definition: Parisi’s 1979 paper replaces a single replica-symmetric spin-glass order parameter with a hierarchy whose infinite limit can be represented by a function on the unit interval.
profile.summary: The starting problem is explicit: the simple Sherrington–Kirkpatrick treatment gives negative zero-temperature entropy and disagrees with simulations. Parisi constructs successively richer replica matrices with one, three, five, and more parameters. Near the critical temperature, a free-energy expansion makes this sequence tractable. The hierarchy is encoded in a piecewise constant function q(x), becoming a function with infinitely many degrees of specification in the limit. Replica symmetry is recovered when the function is constant. The paper notes rapid convergence in the examined expansion but leaves important consistency and interpretation questions open.
profile.why_it_matters: A single average can erase distinctions needed to describe disordered order. The proposed richer description responds to a specific failure of the simpler ansatz, rather than adding complexity for its own sake.
key_distinctions: The model remains the same while its proposed order-parameter structure changes.
Replica symmetry concerns the mathematical treatment of replicas, not a visible geometrical symmetry of a material.
A near-critical expansion does not establish every zero-temperature property.
historical_lineage: The paper explicitly cites Sherrington and Kirkpatrick, de Almeida and Thouless, Bray and Moore, and the Thouless–Anderson–Palmer approach.
logical_antecedents: Replica matrices, analytic continuation towards zero replicas, variational parameters, and the near-transition free-energy expansion.
dependent_subsequents: The closing discussion identifies the physical meaning of q(x), Hessian consistency, and the relation to the Edwards–Anderson parameter as subjects for further investigation.
practice_connections: Curatorial extension: when aggregation fails a concrete diagnostic, identify which lost distinctions a richer representation restores.
common_misreadings: The 1979 letter already provides every later interpretation of overlap structure.
The hierarchy is a general recipe for social or organisational complexity.
open_checks: No independent verification of the replica calculus or later exactness results is claimed.

profile.title: Geometry from a Time Series
profile.canonical_definition: Packard, Crutchfield, Farmer, and Shaw’s 1980 paper demonstrates how a scalar time series can reconstruct aspects of a low-dimensional chaotic attractor using delayed observations or derivatives.
profile.summary: The demonstration samples one coordinate of a three-variable Rössler system. Present and delayed values of that coordinate, or the coordinate with its derivatives, serve as alternative phase-space coordinates. The reconstructed picture is compared with the original attractor. A return-map estimate of a positive characteristic exponent closely matches estimates using the known equations. The paper also proposes conditional-probability methods for estimating the number of independent coordinates needed to specify a state, while distinguishing observed topological structure from fractal dimension.
profile.why_it_matters: A single measured quantity can carry information about unmeasured state variables through its temporal relations. The demonstration gives an operational route from observations to dynamics without claiming that any irregular record reveals a deterministic attractor.
key_distinctions: A scalar measurement is not necessarily a one-dimensional state description.
Geometrical reconstruction differs from recovering the original physical coordinates or governing equations.
The dimensionality seen at finite resolution differs from an attractor’s fractal scaling dimension.
historical_lineage: The paper explicitly starts from Lorenz, Ruelle and Takens, and turbulence experiments, and demonstrates its method on Rössler’s system.
logical_antecedents: A sufficiently informative observable, sampled trajectories, suitable delays or derivative estimates, and adequate resolution.
dependent_subsequents: The article offers reconstruction heuristics and a numerical demonstration; it is not the later general embedding theorem.
practice_connections: Curatorial extension: examine lagged relations before adding independent indicators, while testing noise, non-stationarity, and sampling sensitivity.
common_misreadings: Any delay-coordinate plot proves chaos.
The paper guarantees a universal reconstruction method for actual turbulent data.
open_checks: Validate delay choice, noise sensitivity, and dimensional estimates for each dataset.

profile.title: A Model for the Origin of Life
profile.canonical_definition: Dyson’s 1982 paper constructs a statistical model in which a small, mutually catalytic molecular population can fluctuate from a disordered state into a more catalytically active state.
profile.summary: Each fixed-size island contains active and inactive molecular units. A unit is active when correctly placed within a catalytic structure; its probability of becoming active depends only on the overall active fraction. This mean-field assumption reduces a complicated chemical configuration to a one-dimensional random walk. An assumed response function creates two stable states separated by an unstable threshold. Dyson calculates stationary distributions and transition rates, showing that the waiting time depends exponentially on population size and an effective barrier. Selected illustrative parameters permit transitions for populations of thousands of units.
profile.why_it_matters: The relevant question is the rate of reaching an organised state within finite time, rather than merely its probability in an eventual stationary distribution. The calculation also exposes where chemical knowledge has been replaced by assumptions.
key_distinctions: Activity refers to catalytic placement, not to a molecule being intrinsically alive.
Fixed-size island drift excludes natural selection between growing and reproducing islands.
The response function is chosen for tractability rather than established prebiotic chemistry.
historical_lineage: Dyson explicitly adapts population-genetic reasoning associated with Fisher, Wright, and Kimura, alongside a mean-field analogy from magnetism.
logical_antecedents: Isolated exchanging islands, a fixed unit count, a mutation process, and a catalytic-response function with three crossings.
dependent_subsequents: The questions section conjectures subsequent growth, division, and selection, with a possible enzymes-before-genes interpretation. These are extensions beyond the fixed-size calculation.
practice_connections: Curatorial extension: distinguish transition rates from equilibrium prevalence when judging whether a rare event is feasible.
common_misreadings: The model demonstrates a chemically verified origin of life.
Its parameter examples measure actual early-Earth conditions.
open_checks: Experimental reaction rates and plausible catalytic functions remain necessary for historical claims.

profile.title: Neural Networks and Physical Systems with Emergent Collective Computational Abilities
profile.canonical_definition: Hopfield’s 1982 paper demonstrates how recurrent networks of simple binary units can store patterns as attractors and recover a complete pattern from a sufficiently informative partial or corrupted cue.
profile.summary: Binary neurons update asynchronously according to a threshold on weighted inputs. A correlation-based prescription sets the recurrent connection strengths so that selected patterns tend to become stable states. For symmetric connections, an energy-like function decreases under the update rule until a local minimum is reached. Retrieval is movement through state space towards a stored pattern, rather than looking up a separately addressed record. Simulations investigate recall errors, loading, and departures from symmetry. The paper also reports spurious or altered states and finite storage limits.
profile.why_it_matters: A computational capability can be a property of collective dynamics. The useful result depends on how interactions are arranged and how states update; adding many simple units is insufficient by itself.
key_distinctions: A recurrent attractor network differs from a feedforward mapping.
The symmetric-network energy argument differs from simulated behaviour with asymmetric connections.
A local minimum need not be an intended memory.
historical_lineage: Hopfield explicitly discusses earlier associative matrices, Hebbian correlations, McCulloch–Pitts units, and the analogy with Ising and spin-glass systems.
logical_antecedents: Coded input patterns, specified thresholds and weights, an asynchronous update rule, and a procedure for setting connections.
dependent_subsequents: The model offers a physical interpretation of content-addressable memory, with limited generalisation and robustness in the tested regimes; it is not a complete theory of biological memory.
practice_connections: Curatorial extension: inspect which patterns a recurrent process restores after disturbance, including unintended persistent patterns.
common_misreadings: The network always reaches the desired or globally best state.
Its reported storage fraction is a universal biological capacity law.
open_checks: State the symmetry, loading, coding, and update assumptions before applying convergence or capacity claims.

profile.title: Universal Behavior in Nonlinear Systems
profile.canonical_definition: Feigenbaum’s 1983 account explains universal scaling in a specified period-doubling route to chaos through repeated composition and rescaling of nonlinear maps.
profile.summary: As a parameter changes, a stable cycle can lose stability to a cycle of twice the period, followed by successive doublings. For the class examined, parameter intervals shrink towards a limiting ratio of approximately 4.6692, while spatial separations have a second scaling factor of approximately 2.5029. The explanation studies an operation on functions: compose a map with itself, then rescale it. A fixed function and the stability properties of that operation organise the limiting behaviour. The article connects this construction with continuous oscillators and discusses quantitative comparisons using Duffing’s equation.
profile.why_it_matters: Different detailed equations can share quantitative behaviour when they approach the same limiting structure. The shared numbers follow from a specified universality class rather than from irregularity or nonlinearity alone.
key_distinctions: A fixed point of an ordinary map differs from a fixed function of the composition-and-rescaling operation.
Period doubling is one route to chaos, not the definition of chaos.
The generic quadratic extremum matters; changing that property can change the universality class.
historical_lineage: The article presents Feigenbaum’s scaling programme and compares its fixed-point structure with the theory of critical phenomena; it reprints the 1980 Los Alamos account with additions.
logical_antecedents: A suitable nonlinear map or reduced return map, a tunable parameter, successive cycle instabilities, and the relevant smoothness and extremum assumptions.
dependent_subsequents: The construction yields scaling predictions for maps and selected oscillatory systems; it does not classify every turbulent transition.
practice_connections: Curatorial extension: establish the transition mechanism and class before applying a numerical scaling rule across domains.
common_misreadings: Every chaotic system exhibits the Feigenbaum constant.
Universal scaling supplies long-term trajectory prediction after chaos begins.
open_checks: No independent rigorous proof of the functional fixed-point construction is claimed.

profile.title: Universality and Complexity in Cellular Automata
profile.canonical_definition: Wolfram’s 1984 paper proposes four qualitative classes of one-dimensional cellular-automaton behaviour and investigates their attractors, statistical structure, and potential computational capabilities.
profile.summary: Each lattice site updates synchronously from a finite neighbourhood under a fixed rule. Surveying rules and initial conditions, Wolfram distinguishes homogeneous outcomes, separated simple or periodic structures, chaotic patterns, and persistent complex structures. He analyses these using configuration-space attractors, entropies, dimensions, and grammars. The paper conjectures computational universality for the fourth class and explores consequent limits on general prediction. It repeatedly labels substantial parts of this programme tentative and explicitly says that the treatment is not a rigorous mathematical classification.
profile.why_it_matters: Very short local rules can generate behaviour requiring a different level of description. The paper also separates a deterministic update rule from a practical ability to predict its long-run consequences without carrying it out.
key_distinctions: Rule simplicity differs from simplicity of its generated behaviour.
A finite array eventually repeats and cannot realise unbounded computation.
Evidence for four classes differs from a proof covering every rule and initial condition.
historical_lineage: The article develops Wolfram’s earlier cellular-automaton work and compares attractor behaviour with continuous dynamical systems; universal computation supplies a separate interpretive framework.
logical_antecedents: Specify alphabet, neighbourhood, rule, boundary conditions, initial-state distribution, and observation time.
dependent_subsequents: The class-four discussion proposes links between persistent structures, undecidability, and algorithmic probability; not every conjecture is established in the article.
practice_connections: Curatorial extension: examine several initial conditions and observation windows before assigning a system a qualitative class.
common_misreadings: The paper proves all four classes exhaustive and sharply decidable.
Complex-looking output alone proves computational universality.
open_checks: Keep later results about particular rules separate from the conjectures made in 1984.

profile.title: Self-Organisation in Nonequilibrium Systems: Towards a Dynamics of Complexity
profile.canonical_definition: Prigogine and Nicolis’s 1985 chapter brings thermodynamics, nonlinear dynamics, fluctuations, and experiment together to explain how complex patterns can emerge in systems maintained away from equilibrium.
profile.summary: Dissipation can support reproducible macroscopic structures rather than merely erase order. Distance from equilibrium permits nonlinear kinetic feedbacks to destabilise a reference state; new solution branches can produce oscillations, spatial patterns, multiple alternatives, or chaos. Fluctuations matter near these branching conditions because they can help select which macroscopic path is realised. The authors organise a research programme around thermodynamic constraints, mathematical dynamical structure, stochastic description, and laboratory tests. Their perspective also identifies unresolved questions about chemical self-replication and the origins of biological organisation.
profile.why_it_matters: The account connects an energy-maintained physical organisation to its dynamical and probabilistic description. Thermodynamic permission alone does not specify which pattern appears or when it will change.
key_distinctions: Dissipative structure differs from equilibrium ordering such as a crystal.
A deterministic bifurcation diagram describes possible branches; fluctuations contribute to realised historical outcomes.
Physical sensitivity and history do not by themselves constitute biological life.
historical_lineage: The chapter explicitly discusses Onsager, irreversible-process thermodynamics, dissipative structures, bifurcation theory, and Eigen’s molecular-evolution programme.
logical_antecedents: Open exchange maintaining non-equilibrium conditions, nonlinear evolution equations, control parameters, and a specified fluctuation process.
dependent_subsequents: The programme calls for closer links between global dynamical transitions and experimentally manageable local analysis; it presents possibilities as well as established examples.
practice_connections: Curatorial extension: distinguish the resources sustaining an organised process, its internal feedbacks, and the fluctuations affecting which alternative it takes.
common_misreadings: The second law prohibits local order formation.
Any social disruption is a thermodynamic bifurcation or necessarily creates a better organisation.
open_checks: Use domain-specific mechanisms before carrying the physical analogies into social explanation.

profile.title: Studying Artificial Life with Cellular Automata
profile.canonical_definition: Langton’s 1986 paper uses cellular automata as artificial environments for interacting virtual machines, exploring whether functional relations associated with living chemistry can be realised in another medium.
profile.summary: Local lattice rules support persistent or propagating patterns that can be treated as virtual automata rather than as individual cells. Langton examines their potential to perform molecular roles and presents artificial biochemistries, ant-like agents, and self-reproducing loops. In the loop example, circulating signals are copied at a junction and interpreted as construction instructions at an arm’s end. A daughter receives a complete signal sequence and can reproduce. Neighbouring loops alter available construction space, producing a reproductive fringe and an inactive core.
profile.why_it_matters: The paper makes functional organisation experimentally manipulable. It distinguishes a constructed example of a particular life-like behaviour from the stronger ambition of producing a living, evolving artificial ecology.
key_distinctions: The underlying cellular automaton differs from the virtual machines sustained by its activity.
Information used as construction instructions differs from information copied for a descendant.
A self-reproducing loop need not be a universal constructor or a complete living system.
historical_lineage: Langton explicitly discusses von Neumann’s constructor-and-description logic, Codd’s simplification, Laing’s self-inspection approach, and his own earlier loop construction.
logical_antecedents: Specify lattice rules, initial conditions, persistent signal structures, and an interpretation of their functional roles.
dependent_subsequents: Proposed cooperative colonies, parasitic machines, and variable inherited descriptions remain extensions beyond the demonstrated loop.
practice_connections: Curatorial extension: model local rules and environmental encounters separately from the larger pattern they generate.
common_misreadings: The article proves that its loops are alive.
A successful simulation establishes that natural biochemistry uses the same mechanism.

profile.title: Fusion, Propagation, and Structuring in Belief Networks
profile.canonical_definition: Pearl's 1986 paper represents uncertain knowledge with directed acyclic graphs and conditional probabilities, and develops distributed procedures for updating beliefs and reconstructing certain hidden tree structures.
profile.summary: The graph encodes conditional independencies; numerical tables specify local dependencies. For singly connected networks, neighbouring processors exchange separately tracked sources of support until beliefs agree with probability theory. The distinction between fixed link probabilities and changing beliefs is central. A second part investigates when observable dependencies permit a tree representation using hidden variables. Graph structure helps make inference tractable, but the favourable propagation result depends on the topology.
profile.why_it_matters: An uncertainty model becomes an executable inference architecture. The paper explains why evidence sources must be kept separate to avoid counting their support repeatedly.
key_distinctions: An arrow can represent inferential association as well as causation; direction alone doesn't establish a causal claim.
Updating beliefs with new evidence differs from learning the network's parameters or structure.
historical_lineage: The paper develops probabilistic expert-system research and discusses alternatives based on connectionist relaxation.
logical_antecedents: A joint probability model, conditional independence, and an explicit graph topology.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about local message passing, diagnostic explanation, and hidden-variable modelling.
practice_connections: Curatorial application: in a decision model, record which observations support which claims and what independence assumptions justify combining them. A diagram without probability assignments isn't the method described here.

profile.summary: Replication rates, degradation, and copying errors define a value matrix. Localisation, shifts between quasi-species, and the final error threshold are distinct phenomena.

logical_antecedents: Error-prone replication, an explicit sequence space, and a defined replication-mutation matrix.

Deterministic large-population results don't remove stochastic losses in small populations.

profile.title: Competing Technologies, Increasing Returns, and Lock-In by Historical Events
profile.canonical_definition: Arthur's 1989 paper models how increasing returns to adoption can amplify early choices and lock a market into one competing technology, including a technology with inferior unrealised long-run potential.
profile.summary: Two types of adopters have different initial preferences. Their sequential choices also depend on accumulated adoption, which changes pay-offs. With increasing returns, a sufficiently large early lead can make both types choose the same technology; the resulting dynamics have absorbing barriers. Arthur contrasts this with constant and diminishing returns and separates predictability, flexibility, ergodicity, and path efficiency. historical_lineage: The paper's earlier working-paper history is stated, and learning-by-using research supplies its motivation.
logical_antecedents: Sequential adoption, heterogeneous preferences, and returns that depend on adoption history.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about technological standards, expectations, policy timing, and switching costs.

profile.canonical_definition: Holland and Miller's 1991 paper proposes executable models of interacting adaptive agents as a way to investigate economic learning, novelty, and emergent aggregate behaviour.
profile.summary: Agents have evaluable actions and mechanisms that improve their performance over time; other adapting agents form part of each agent's environment. The paper explains how genetic algorithms search among encoded structures and how classifier systems combine condition-action rules, credit assignment, and rule discovery. Controlled artificial experiments can reset learning and vary assumptions. The authors also identify a central difficulty: conclusions may depend on which learning algorithm is chosen.
profile.why_it_matters: The contribution is a research method and programme. Inspectable artificial mechanisms permit questions that equilibrium solutions alone leave unanswered, while sensitivity across agent designs remains necessary.
key_distinctions: An adaptive agent isn't simply an agent executing fixed behaviour.
An internally consistent executable model still needs a plausibility check and comparison with established results.
historical_lineage: The paper develops Holland's genetic-algorithm and classifier-system research in economic modelling.
logical_antecedents: Explicit agents, interaction rules, a performance criterion, and a learning mechanism.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about equilibrium selection, decentralised learning, new niches, and robust aggregate results.
practice_connections: Curatorial application: use repeatable artificial experiments to test whether an outcome depends on a proposed learning mechanism. Retain the difference between behaviour inside an artificial world and evidence about an actual economy.
common_misreadings: The authors explicitly propose complementing existing economic theory, rather than replacing every analytical method.
The ability to produce emergent behaviour doesn't by itself validate a model.
open_checks: Test robustness across algorithmic choices; the paper offers no completed general calculus of adaptive mechanics.

profile.title: Evolutionary Phenomena in Simple Dynamics
profile.canonical_definition: Lindgren's 1991 model evolves finite-memory strategies for a noisy iterated prisoner's dilemma, allowing the strategy space itself to expand through mutations that change memory length.
profile.summary: Individuals play against the population, and successful strategies leave more offspring. Binary genomes encode responses to finite histories; point mutations alter responses, while duplication and splitting change memory capacity. Mistakes make retaliation and recovery consequential. Simulations display long stasis interrupted by rapid changes, cooperative partnerships between distinct strategies, and population collapses arising within the dynamics. The conclusion distinguishes finding a stable successful strategy from maintaining an open-ended evolutionary process.
profile.why_it_matters: A model can generate abrupt evolutionary-looking changes without an external catastrophe. That is a demonstration of possibility within the model, not a reconstruction of a biological extinction.
key_distinctions: An intended deterministic strategy differs from the noisy action actually performed.
The strategies available to evolution aren't restricted to the initial four memory-one types.
historical_lineage: The paper explicitly develops the repeated-game tradition of Axelrod and Maynard Smith and Price, and compares its stasis with punctuated equilibrium.
logical_antecedents: A pay-off matrix, strategy encoding, mutation operators, population selection, and action noise.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about endogenous instability, evolving memory, mutualism, and cooperative robustness.
practice_connections: Curatorial application: examine whether changing participants and strategies can generate the apparent disruption attributed to an outside event. Any organisational comparison needs its own evidence and explicit interaction rules.
common_misreadings: The result doesn't prove that real mass extinctions are internally caused.
Tit-for-tat's performance in a noiseless tournament doesn't settle its robustness under mistakes and evolving opponents.
open_checks: Check the noise, pay-offs, population assumptions, and permitted mutations before transferring any stable-strategy claim.

profile.title: Organizations and Markets
profile.canonical_definition: Simon's 1991 paper argues that an economy composed largely of organisations needs an account of authority, rewards, identification, and coordination alongside the theory of market exchange.
profile.summary: Employment leaves many future actions unspecified, allowing decisions to be made when circumstances are clearer. Authority commonly supplies goals, constraints, and decision premises rather than detailed orders. Simon examines why employees contribute beyond minimally enforceable effort and treats organisational identification as a substantive mechanism. He also shows how specialised knowledge can enter decisions through multiple channels. Markets and organisations are therefore alternative and interacting ways to coordinate activity.
profile.why_it_matters: The paper makes the internal working of organisations part of economic explanation. Assuming contractual incentives alone can miss how people understand their tasks and whose purposes they advance.
key_distinctions: Authority over decision premises differs from specifying every action.
Organisational identification can support collective effort and can also narrow attention towards a department's goals.
historical_lineage: The paper develops Simon's earlier work on employment, administrative behaviour, and bounded human decision-making.
logical_antecedents: Uncertain future tasks, delegated decisions, social motivation, and interdependent work.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about firm boundaries, departmental goals, public organisations, and coordination costs.
practice_connections: Practice connection: examine the premises, information, and local goals that shape delegated decisions. Simon's argument applies explicitly to private, nonprofit, and government organisations; it isn't a presumption that every hierarchy works well.
common_misreadings: The paper doesn't explain obedience as the passive execution of commands.
It doesn't establish that organisations always outperform markets.
open_checks: Compare the proposed motivational mechanisms with evidence from the particular organisation being studied.

profile.title: Emergent Properties of Balinese Water Temple Networks: Coadaptation on a Rugged Fitness Landscape
profile.canonical_definition: Lansing and Kremer's 1993 paper uses ecological and adaptive simulations to examine how Balinese farmers' coordination of cropping can manage competing demands for water and pest control.
profile.summary: Synchronising fallow periods suppresses pests, while synchronising irrigation demand can worsen water shortages. An ecological model represents these interacting constraints. In a second model, each subak compares harvests with neighbours and copies the most successful neighbouring cropping pattern. Repeated adjustment produces coordinated patches resembling temple networks and improves modelled harvests. Simulated disturbance responses are properties of the resulting network as well as individual decisions.
profile.why_it_matters: The coordination problem has a variable scale. Wider synchronisation can help one ecological process while harming another, so neither complete independence nor universal uniformity is assumed best.
key_distinctions: Artificial temple networks are model outcomes, distinguished explicitly from actual religious institutions.
Coadaptation finds locally favourable coordination patterns; it doesn't demonstrate a global optimum or establish the institutions' actual historical origin.
historical_lineage: The authors connect field investigation, ecological simulation, and coevolving fitness landscapes, while explicitly addressing human intention.
logical_antecedents: Water flows, pest dynamics, cropping schedules, local comparison, and adaptive copying.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about coordination scale, institutional resilience, and the interaction of social and ecological change.
practice_connections: Practice connection: preserve the specific water–pest trade-off when using this case. Curatorial application elsewhere: identify the different processes whose coordination scales conflict; copying temple structures supplies no general solution.
common_misreadings: Self-organisation here doesn't mean an absence of deliberate local decisions.
Simulation resemblance isn't sufficient historical evidence for how real water temples developed.
open_checks: Check validation data and alternative social mechanisms before claiming the model explains all of Balinese irrigation.

profile.title: Revisiting the Edge of Chaos: Evolving Cellular Automata to Perform Computations
profile.canonical_definition: Mitchell, Hraber, and Crutchfield's 1993 paper tests whether evolving cellular automata for a density-classification task supports a claimed link between computational capability and the 'edge of chaos'.
profile.summary: A genetic algorithm evolves local update tables to classify whether a binary lattice initially contains a majority of ones. The experiments yield different results from the earlier study they revisit. The authors analyse competing computational strategies and show how symmetry breaking can impede improvement. Their discussion distinguishes performance on a task, capacity for universal computation under special initial conditions, and intrinsic information processing. Langton's lambda parameter doesn't provide an independent measure of these capacities.
profile.why_it_matters: The paper requires 'computational capability' and 'edge of chaos' to be made testable. Attractive global patterns or a coarse parameter aren't substitutes for measuring the task actually performed.
key_distinctions: A cellular automaton's dynamical class differs from the computation attributed to it.
The lambda parameter is a property of a rule table; it doesn't uniquely identify behaviour across initial conditions.
historical_lineage: The study explicitly revisits Packard's experiment and Langton's hypotheses, drawing on Wolfram's classifications.
logical_antecedents: A defined task, fitness evaluation, genetic search, and a distinction between rule-space and behaviour.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about emergent computational strategies, symmetry, and observer-dependent filters.
practice_connections: Curatorial application: before using 'edge of chaos' as advice, identify a measured capability and a falsifiable relationship. The paper provides no direct experiment on organisational performance.
common_misreadings: It doesn't show that useful computation is impossible near critical transitions.
Its critique shouldn't become an unrestricted rejection of all criticality hypotheses.
open_checks: The original 1993 study must be distinguished from the authors' later 1997 account of evolving cellular automata.

profile.title: Inductive Reasoning and Bounded Rationality
profile.canonical_definition: Arthur's 1994 paper models bounded rationality through agents that hold, evaluate, and replace several provisional forecasting models, illustrated by the El Farol bar-attendance problem.
profile.summary: One hundred agents choose whether to attend a bar that is enjoyable below a crowding threshold. They observe past attendance and act on their currently best-performing predictor. A universally shared forecast would defeat itself: expecting low attendance makes everyone go, while expecting high attendance makes everyone stay home. The resulting population of predictors changes as agents learn. The example demonstrates how heterogeneous expectations and aggregate regularities can coexist.
profile.why_it_matters: Agents' forecasts help create the environment they are forecasting. Learning therefore concerns a moving set of other people's expectations, rather than merely estimating fixed external parameters.
key_distinctions: Provisional useful beliefs aren't guaranteed to be true.
The reported simulation is a constructed illustration; it isn't an empirical test of actual bar-goers or a theorem covering every learning rule.
historical_lineage: Arthur explicitly credits Holland's work and relates the model to psychological accounts of induction.
logical_antecedents: Limited information, alternative predictor models, performance feedback, and interdependent decisions.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about model turnover, coordination, and aggregate behaviour under heterogeneous expectations.
practice_connections: Curatorial application: when publishing a forecast, ask whether people acting on it will change the outcome. Compare several hypotheses and retain a record of their performance; the bar model doesn't choose the right forecasting method for an organisation.
common_misreadings: Bounded rationality doesn't mean arbitrary behaviour or the abandonment of reasoning.
A stable-looking aggregate doesn't mean individual models have stopped changing.
open_checks: Test sensitivity to predictor generation and updating rules before generalising the simulation.

profile.title: The Calculi of Emergence: Computation, Dynamics, and Induction
profile.canonical_definition: Crutchfield's 1994 paper develops computational mechanics as a way to infer a process's predictive structure and to examine emergence through changes in the model classes available to an observer.
profile.summary: Histories with the same conditional predictions are grouped into causal states; their transitions form an epsilon-machine. Statistical complexity measures the information stored in that predictive representation, distinguishing structure from sheer unpredictability. The paper extends incremental reconstruction towards hierarchical reconstruction, where regularities in one model motivate a richer representation. Finite measurement and inference resources help determine what the observer detects. Examples include dynamical transitions, hidden stochastic processes, and filtered cellular-automaton patterns.
profile.why_it_matters: Calling a pattern new depends partly on the descriptive resources used to look for it. The paper supplies a technical programme for examining that dependence rather than treating observer judgement as an unexplained exception.
key_distinctions: High entropy doesn't necessarily mean high statistical complexity.
The paper distinguishes intuitive novelty, observer-identified pattern formation, and intrinsic emergence in which a system exploits patterns.
historical_lineage: The argument connects dynamical systems, information theory, computation theory, and inductive inference.
logical_antecedents: Time-series measurements, conditional future distributions, a model class, and finite inference resources.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about predictive memory, changing representations, and hidden structure in apparently random behaviour.
practice_connections: Curatorial application: state what data and model class make an organisational pattern visible, and what would count as a better predictive representation. The formal reconstruction method requires much more than noticing a theme.
common_misreadings: A causal state is a predictive equivalence class; it doesn't by itself identify an intervention-based physical cause.
A compelling visual pattern isn't an independently measured computational mechanism.
open_checks: Check the process assumptions, measurement resolution, and finite-data reconstruction error before using a complexity estimate.

profile.title: Self–Nonself Discrimination in a Computer
profile.canonical_definition: Forrest and colleagues' 1994 paper adapts immune negative selection into a computer change-detection algorithm: generate candidate detectors and discard those that match protected 'self' data.
profile.summary: Protected data are represented as strings. Random candidate strings that avoid matching self become detectors; a later match signals a change. Partial matching across contiguous positions makes detection feasible without enumerating all possible altered strings. The paper analyses detection probabilities and generation costs, and reports preliminary file-change experiments. Different detector sets can distribute checking, with a trade-off between cost and detection quality.
profile.why_it_matters: The algorithm detects departures from a baseline without specifying every harmful change in advance. Its limits make the analogy concrete: training must begin with uncorrupted self, coverage is probabilistic, and deletions aren't noticed by the described procedure.
key_distinctions: A detected change isn't automatically a malicious virus.
The paper offers an algorithm and preliminary feasibility tests, rather than a fully deployed security system.
historical_lineage: The authors explicitly adapt the generation and censoring of immune T cells into a computer-security problem.
logical_antecedents: A trustworthy stable baseline, string segmentation, a matching rule, and adequate detector coverage.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about distributed detection, blind spots, detector-generation cost, and changing definitions of self.
practice_connections: Curatorial application: for any anomaly-detection scheme, specify how the baseline was certified and what changes remain invisible. Biological language doesn't remove those engineering questions.
common_misreadings: Negative selection isn't a complete simulation of an immune system.
Absence of a detector match doesn't guarantee that a protected file is unchanged.
open_checks: Assess adversarial changes, baseline drift, and practical generation costs before using this historical method in an actual security design.

profile.title: From Sequences to Shapes and Back: A Case Study in RNA Secondary Structures
profile.canonical_definition: Schuster and colleagues' 1994 paper examines how many RNA sequences map to the same secondary structure, and how that many-to-one map changes the possibilities for evolutionary search.
profile.summary: Minimum-free-energy folding maps sequence space into a smaller, unevenly populated shape space. Computational sampling and inverse folding indicate relatively few common structures and many rare ones. Neutral paths connect sequences that retain a structure, while local sequence neighbourhoods can contain many common alternative shapes. Thus structural robustness and access to alternatives can coexist. The authors explicitly qualify their thermodynamic folding criterion, use of one minimum-energy structure, and omission of full three-dimensional structure.
profile.why_it_matters: The accessibility of a phenotype depends on the mapping from sequences to shapes, not just the number of possible sequences. Neutral change can relocate a population without changing the measured phenotype.
key_distinctions: Neutrality here preserves the chosen secondary-structure description, not necessarily every biological function.
A common structure's accessibility differs from the ease of finding an arbitrary rare structure.
historical_lineage: The article connects RNA folding, sequence-space geometry, molecular quasi-species, and Maynard Smith's discussion of neutral networks.
logical_antecedents: A sequence metric, a folding rule, a structural representation, and defined mutation moves.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about robust genotypes, neutral exploration, inverse design, and genotype–phenotype bias.
practice_connections: Curatorial application: when many designs produce the same measured outcome, examine which alternatives become reachable after apparently neutral changes. Applying this to institutions requires evidence for the relevant equivalence and neighbourhood.
common_misreadings: Neutral networks don't mean mutations are universally harmless.
The results aren't a direct map of RNA's complete three-dimensional functional landscape.
open_checks: Check folding kinetics, structural ensembles, chain length, and functional assays before translating accessibility into biological performance.

profile.title: Information Measures, Effective Complexity, and Total Information
profile.canonical_definition: Gell-Mann and Lloyd's 1996 paper defines effective complexity as the concise description of an entity's identified regularities, and total information as that description plus an entropy term for its remaining variability.
profile.summary: An entity is embedded as a typical member of an ensemble representing its perceived regularities. The ensemble's algorithmic information content measures effective complexity; its entropy describes residual uncertainty. Random strings can have high algorithmic information while being effectively simple. To compare descriptions, the authors propose minimising total information and then effective complexity, subject to computational constraints. They also analyse how coarse-graining and the observer's description enter the construction.
profile.why_it_matters: Different quantities answer different questions about information. Counting unpredictability, counting regularities, and specifying one individual object should not be silently treated as the same measure of complexity.
key_distinctions: Effective complexity concerns the regularities' description, not the shortest program for the individual string alone.
The choice of ensemble, detail, language, and coding convention affects the initial description.
historical_lineage: The paper combines Shannon information, statistical mechanics, algorithmic information theory, and earlier Gell-Mann complexity proposals.
logical_antecedents: A specified entity, computable ensemble, typicality condition, and resource-bounded description.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about model selection, regularity, noise, and observer dependence.

profile.title: Niche Construction
profile.canonical_definition: Odling-Smee, Laland, and Feldman's 1996 article argues that organisms' modifications of their environments can alter selection pressures and transmit an ecological inheritance to later generations.
profile.summary: The examples include earthworms changing soils, animals constructing nests, and culturally mediated changes in human environments. The article separates repeatedly reconstructed conditions from environmental consequences that persist across generations. Feedback through modified resources can affect genetic loci other than those producing the original niche-construction behaviour, including across species. Delays in accumulated environmental effects can create evolutionary momentum after an initiating pressure changes.
profile.why_it_matters: Adaptation's environment can be partly a product of organisms' past activity. The article asks evolutionary analysis to include that feedback and its inheritance rather than treating every selective condition as externally supplied.
key_distinctions: Niche construction can arise from metabolic by-products, learning, or culture; intention isn't required.
Ecological inheritance isn't a claim that environmental change rewrites the inherited DNA sequence.
historical_lineage: Lewontin's organism–environment argument, Darwin's earthworm observations, and earlier ecological-inheritance proposals are explicit antecedents.
logical_antecedents: Environmental modification that changes a source of selection, and a mechanism linking it to subsequent populations.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about delayed selection, indirect genetic interactions, coevolution, and inherited environmental legacies.
practice_connections: Curatorial application: inspect how today's work changes the conditions inherited by successors. An organisational application is an analogy unless the relevant environmental persistence and selection processes are independently specified.
common_misreadings: Every environmental effect isn't necessarily a demonstrated evolutionary cause.
The article argues for a wider theory; it doesn't provide a complete quantitative model for all its examples.

profile.title: A General Model for the Origin of Allometric Scaling Laws in Biology
profile.canonical_definition: West, Brown, and Enquist's 1997 paper proposes that biological quarter-power scaling can arise from the geometry and transport physics of branching resource-distribution networks.
profile.summary: The model combines three assumptions: a space-filling branching network, terminal units that remain approximately invariant with organism size, and minimisation of transport energy. It relates network structure to metabolic demand and develops separate treatments of steady and pulsatile flow. A simple area-preserving geometry gives a three-quarter exponent, but mammalian circulation needs the pulsatile analysis to reconcile that scaling with slowing flow towards capillaries. The authors compare predicted quantities with biological data.
profile.why_it_matters: The proposed exponent is attached to a mechanism and explicit constraints. A fitted power law alone wouldn't establish that resource-network mechanism.
key_distinctions: Geometric branching within one organism differs from scaling between organisms of different sizes.
The paper calls the network idealised and omits complications such as vessel tapering, turbulence, and nonlinear junction effects.
historical_lineage: The article combines biological allometry, fractal-like branching geometry, and earlier flow-optimisation work including Murray's law.
logical_antecedents: Conserved flow, terminal-unit assumptions, space filling, and specified transport costs.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about metabolic rates, vessel dimensions, network efficiency, and the scope of scaling exponents.
practice_connections: Curatorial application: when invoking an economy-of-scale law, identify what flows, how it is distributed, and which terminal requirements remain fixed. Extending a biological exponent to organisations requires a separate model and evidence.
common_misreadings: The model doesn't establish that every biological quantity has an exact quarter-power exponent.
A fractal-looking diagram doesn't prove the energy-minimisation assumption.
open_checks: Review later empirical tests and critiques before treating the 1997 model's universality claims as settled.

profile.title: No Free Lunch Theorems for Optimization
profile.canonical_definition: Wolpert and Macready's 1997 paper proves equalities in black-box search performance when results are averaged uniformly over all cost functions in a specified finite optimisation setting.
profile.summary: An algorithm selects new points after observing previous function evaluations. Performance is measured from the values found after a fixed number of distinct evaluations. Under uniform averaging, an advantage on one collection of functions is offset elsewhere. The paper then examines nonuniform distributions over problems, geometric alignment between algorithms and problem distributions, benchmark interpretation, and distinctions that remain in head-to-head comparisons. Time-dependent cases require their own assumptions.
profile.why_it_matters: Good search depends on a relationship between the method and the problems encountered. The theorem motivates stating that relationship; it doesn't say useful optimisation is impossible.
key_distinctions: Uniform averaging over all functions differs from the structured, nonuniform problem classes practitioners face.
The paper counts distinct oracle evaluations; it doesn't establish equal wall-clock time or implementation cost.
historical_lineage: The work connects black-box optimisation, information theory, and earlier no-free-lunch results in learning.
logical_antecedents: Finite search and value spaces, an explicit algorithm model, and a specified performance measure and problem distribution.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about benchmark representativeness, prior structure, and method–problem matching.
practice_connections: Practice connection: report the problem class behind a performance comparison and justify why it resembles the intended use. Curatorial transfer beyond computational search should be labelled an analogy, not a theorem about all management methods.
common_misreadings: No free lunch doesn't mean all algorithms perform equally on every individual problem.
It doesn't remove advantages gained from exploitable structure or domain knowledge.

profile.title: Natural Gradient Works Efficiently in Learning
profile.canonical_definition: Amari's 1998 paper defines a natural gradient that follows steepest local change with respect to a parameter space's metric, using information geometry to derive learning rules.
profile.summary: In a curved or nonorthonormal parameter space, the ordinary coordinate gradient doesn't give the metric's steepest direction. Multiplying it by the inverse metric gives the natural gradient. For statistical models, the Fisher information supplies that metric. The paper derives forms for neural networks, blind source separation, and source deconvolution. Its asymptotic efficiency result concerns a specified online estimator with a realisable teacher and a one-over-time learning rate.
profile.why_it_matters: The notion of a small step depends on the space in which change is measured. An optimisation rule can therefore depend on geometry rather than the arbitrary scaling of parameter coordinates.
key_distinctions: A Riemannian steepest direction is a local result, distinct from global convergence.
Fisher efficiency is asymptotic statistical accuracy under stated conditions; it isn't a promise of minimum computation or universal faster training.
historical_lineage: The paper develops information geometry, earlier natural-gradient work, and stochastic approximation theory.
logical_antecedents: A differentiable loss, a valid metric, an invertible Fisher matrix where used, and the learning assumptions.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about parametrisation, efficient estimation, adaptive learning rates, and plateaux.
practice_connections: Practice connection: in statistical learning, check the metric and its computational cost alongside the update rule. Curatorial analogy elsewhere: equal numerical changes in different parameters may represent unequal substantive changes; that alone doesn't justify applying this algorithm.
common_misreadings: An arbitrary positive-definite preconditioner isn't automatically the Fisher natural gradient.
The paper suggests improved plateau behaviour; it doesn't prove every plateau disappears.
open_checks: Check regularity, model misspecification, singularity, and finite-step behaviour before using the efficiency claim.

profile.title: Endogenous Preferences: The Cultural Consequences of Markets and Other Economic Institutions
profile.canonical_definition: Bowles's 1998 review argues that economic institutions can shape preferences, values, and behavioural dispositions as well as allocate goods among people with already fixed wants.
profile.summary: The paper reviews evidence and models from several disciplines. It examines how institutions frame situations, structure rewards, influence norms, organise tasks, and alter cultural transmission. The same choice set may evoke different conduct when presented as a market transaction or a social relationship. Work experience may also shape dispositions beyond work. Bowles distinguishes these mechanisms and identifies unresolved questions about causal direction, persistence, and empirical magnitude.
profile.why_it_matters: A policy can change the behaviour and preferences on which its own evaluation depends. Fixed-preference analysis can therefore leave out part of the institutional effect.
key_distinctions: Short-term framing of a choice differs from a lasting change in preferences.
Evidence that institutions matter doesn't imply that every market creates selfishness or that all nonmarket institutions encourage cooperation.
historical_lineage: The review places the exogenous-preference assumption beside social learning, cultural evolution, experimental economics, and sociological evidence.
logical_antecedents: A specified institutional arrangement, a plausible transmission mechanism, and evidence separating selection from socialisation.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about incentives, norm crowding, work design, and evaluating institutions when preferences change.
practice_connections: Practice connection: assess what habits and expectations a payment, monitoring rule, or job design may teach as well as its immediate allocation effect. The paper itself cautions against confidence in deliberate psychological engineering.
common_misreadings: Observed differences between groups don't automatically establish institutions as their cause.
Preference endogeneity isn't permission to invent convenient preferences to explain any result.
open_checks: Check long-term persistence and causal identification; the conclusion explicitly calls for stronger empirical work.

profile.title: Collective Dynamics of 'Small-World' Networks
profile.canonical_definition: Watts and Strogatz's 1998 paper shows that networks can combine strong local clustering with short paths between distant nodes, and explores consequences for dynamics.
profile.summary: Starting from a regular ring lattice, the model randomly rewires a fraction of edges while keeping node and edge counts fixed. A few long-range shortcuts sharply reduce characteristic path length while leaving much local clustering intact. The authors compare three observed networks with random benchmarks, then simulate disease spread and report further computational, game, and synchronisation examples. They explicitly simplify empirical edges as undirected and unweighted.
profile.why_it_matters: Local neighbourhoods can appear almost unchanged while routes across the whole network shorten. The same structural change can accelerate useful transmission and undesirable contagion.
key_distinctions: Short average paths alone don't define the paper's small-world combination; clustering also matters.
The dynamical consequences depend on the process: shortcuts don't improve every collective outcome.
historical_lineage: The paper joins small-world social-network questions with coupled dynamical systems and random-graph comparisons.
logical_antecedents: A defined graph, a rewiring procedure, path-length and clustering measures, and a specific dynamical rule.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about diffusion, synchronisation, computation, and robust comparison with network benchmarks.
practice_connections: Curatorial application: identify which distant groups a proposed connection joins and what travels over it. A new link's effects cannot be assessed merely by counting the participants' immediate contacts.
common_misreadings: The model isn't a claim that every network is scale-free.
Small-world topology doesn't by itself demonstrate trust, cooperation, or beneficial coordination.

profile.title: The Middle Way
profile.canonical_definition: Laughlin and colleagues' 'The Middle Way' proposes an experimental and theoretical search for organising principles at mesoscopic scales, between atomic descriptions and bulk behaviour.
profile.summary: The argument begins with collective properties such as ferromagnetism and superconductivity that remain stable against small changes in microscopic details. It asks whether comparable 'protected' organisation exists at intermediate scales in biological and nonbiological matter. Examples include proteins, glasses, amphiphilic structures, and correlated-electron materials. The authors discuss candidate concepts, including energy landscapes, frustration, and feedback, while stressing the shortage of probes that can reveal the relevant organisation.
profile.why_it_matters: Knowing microscopic laws doesn't by itself deliver a tractable prediction of every aggregate. The paper nevertheless leaves mesoscopic organising principles as questions for experimental discovery and possible disproof.
key_distinctions: A proposed mesoscopic principle differs from an established macroscopic example.
The authors accept microscopic physical rules while questioning whether those rules alone provide a usable explanation at every scale.
historical_lineage: Anderson's 'More Is Different' is explicitly cited, alongside condensed-matter and biological research.
logical_antecedents: A defined observational scale, collective behaviour, and tests of robustness to microscopic changes.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about effective theories, measurement limits, and the relation between physical organisation and biological function.
practice_connections: Curatorial application: ask which level of description gives a stable explanation of the behaviour being studied. This methodological comparison doesn't establish physical 'protectorates' in organisations or excuse abandoning empirical detail.
common_misreadings: The paper doesn't prove that all mesoscopic systems obey a new universal law.
'Emergence' here isn't evidence that collective behaviour violates underlying physics.

profile.title: Collective Action and the Evolution of Social Norms
profile.canonical_definition: Ostrom's 2000 paper explains collective action using a heterogeneous population of rational egoists, conditional cooperators, and willing punishers, and examines how norms and institutional rules support cooperation.
profile.summary: Laboratory findings challenge the prediction of universal non-contribution. An indirect evolutionary approach distinguishes material pay-offs from preferences governing choices; information about others' trustworthiness affects which types persist. The paper connects this argument to field evidence and design principles for durable common-resource institutions. Local rule-making, accountable monitoring, graduated sanctions, and conflict-resolution arrangements help sustain reciprocity. Their effects depend on the resource, group, and wider setting.
profile.why_it_matters: Cooperation can depend on both learned expectations and rules people can help shape. Changing enforcement can also change norms, so a policy's behavioural effects may outlast its immediate incentives.
key_distinctions: Conditional cooperation depends on enough others reciprocating; it isn't unconditional altruism.
Design principles describe recurrent features of long-surviving regimes, not one identical rulebook for every resource.
historical_lineage: The paper revisits Olson's collective-action problem and builds on evolutionary models, experiments, and Ostrom's earlier field research.
logical_antecedents: Interdependent pay-offs, heterogeneous motivations, information about conduct, and opportunities to make and enforce rules.
dependent_subsequents: Questions about trust, monitoring, norm crowding, local autonomy, and institutional durability.
practice_connections: Practice connection: examine who can change rules, how conduct becomes visible, and how proportionate sanctions work. The paper warns that weak externally imposed enforcement can undermine existing cooperation; it doesn't claim external authority is always harmful.
common_misreadings: Self-organisation doesn't mean no rules, monitoring, or legitimate authority.
Observed cooperation doesn't remove free-riding or guarantee that a local regime is fair.
open_checks: Use the design principles diagnostically and check local power and exclusion; don't infer a universal success recipe.
